title: Ulyana and the Room
premise: Yara Eriksen arrives at Blackfen Secondary to replace a teacher who vanished mid-term, and finds a school where one classroom, Room 4, has been quietly erased from every record since 1974. Her compulsive documentation begins recording things she never wrote: attendance lists of children who don't exist, and a signature line waiting for the name of whoever agrees to 'close the file.' The room survives by feeding on institutional forgetting, and it needs a living resident to sign away its last stolen child before it can finally die. Yara discovers the missing teacher didn't flee — she signed, trading herself to keep the class of 1974 sealed inside. In the end, Yara refuses to sign and instead returns what was taken: she carries the room's ledger of names into daylight, forcing the town to remember, which starves the room until it releases the children and collapses; the cost is that Yara's own documented memories of her sister begin fading from every page she ever wrote.
about_author: Hazel Dunmore is the pen name of a former school archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing records no one ever requested. She writes horror about institutions, believing the scariest buildings are the ones with perfect filing systems.

chapters.title: The Induction Folder
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She arrives at Blackfen with labeled binders and a ritual of documenting everything, a habit born after her sister's unsolved disappearance. The welcome pack contains no floor plan for the east wing. Emotional beat: controlled optimism curdling into first unease.

chapters.title: Room 3B
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Her timetable lists her in Room 3B, but the door is stenciled 4, and inside the desks are arranged for thirty students though her roster holds twenty-nine. A chalkboard bears half-erased arithmetic dated June 1974. Beat: rationalization under pressure.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Taking register, she reads out a thirtieth name — Ida Voss — before catching herself; the class goes silent, one boy mouths 'don't say it again.' That night her documentation notebook contains an entry she didn't write. Beat: dread entering the domestic.

chapters.title: The Colleague Who Was Here Before You
chapters.summary: POV shifts to caretaker Dennis Okafor, who has worked at Blackfen forty years. He warns Yara obliquely about the east wing and mentions her predecessor, Miss Aldridge, 'who handed in her notice without handing in herself.' Beat: the institution's complicit memory.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. At home, every mirror begins reflecting her kitchen one second behind reality — a kettle whistling before she lifts it, her own face arriving late. She documents the lag obsessively; the timestamps in her notes are wrong by exactly one second too. Beat: reality's seam splitting open.

chapters.title: Through the Glass
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The mirror shows Room 4 as it was in 1974, children at desks, a woman at the board writing names. When Yara reaches toward the glass, the room reaches back, and she is pulled through into the middle of the lesson, where all thirty children turn and look at her. Beat: threshold crossed, terror and strange belonging.

chapters.title: The Class of 1974
chapters.summary: Inside the room, Yara learns the children were taken during a fire drill that never ended; the room ate their exit. Ida Voss, smallest and oldest-seeming, explains the rule: someone outside must return what was taken, or the last resident signs the papers. Beat: horror reframed as custody dispute over souls.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Dennis's POV. He retrieves a locked box from the boiler room: the original 1974 incident file, pulled from archives by the headmaster's office decades ago. Inside are photographs of thirty children and a deed of conveyance — the school legally 'acquired' the classroom's contents, including the pupils' names. Beat: banal evil in triplicate.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She realizes Miss Aldridge is still inside the room, aged wrong, kept as 'resident' because she signed in 1998 to stop the room spreading. Aldridge begs her not to fix anything: the papers need only one more signature and the room closes forever — with everyone in it. Beat: mercy weaponized.

chapters.title: Headmaster Halloway
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. The current headmaster knows everything; his predecessors have managed the room like an asset, using it to dispose of problems — including, he implies, people who asked about Yara's sister. He offers Yara a promotion and a warning. Beat: power showing its face politely.

chapters.title: The Sister Thread
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Cross-referencing her own archive against the 1974 photos, she finds her sister's name on a later intake list — the room has been taking one child per decade, and the paperwork was always signed by a teacher trying to contain it. Beat: grief weaponized into purpose.

chapters.title: Signatures
chapters.summary: Dennis's POV. Dennis confesses he witnessed the 1974 drill as a boy and ran when told to; his survival was the room's first payment. He gives Yara the box and tells her the truth isn't in the file — it's in returning the file to the town that filed it away. Beat: guilt transmuted into testimony.

chapters.title: Erasure
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The room retaliates: entries vanish from her notebooks, colleagues forget her mid-conversation, her flat's lease shows no tenant. Documentation, her prayer, is being answered with silence. She starts copying everything in duplicate and hiding copies off-site. Beat: identity under siege.

chapters.title: The Papers Arrive
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. Under pressure from governors who sense something is wrong, Halloway decides to end it the clean way: he'll sign the papers himself, closing the room permanently and sealing his career's darkest convenience forever. The documents materialize on his desk, pre-filled, patient. Beat: corruption choosing efficiency over conscience.

chapters.title: Aldridge's Bargain
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Inside the room, Aldridge reveals the loophole: the papers can be refused if what was taken is returned first — the names must be given back to the living, spoken publicly, remembered. But the room will take a keeper in exchange for every name returned. Beat: hope priced in flesh.

chapters.title: Assembly
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Yara hijacks morning assembly, reading the thirty names aloud over the PA while Dennis unlocks the east wing and parents arrive demanding answers. The mirrors across town flicker; the room convulses as each name lands. Halloway moves to cut the power. Beat: justice staged outside the law.

chapters.title: The Signing
chapters.summary: Climax, Yara's POV. Halloway signs anyway — but the papers reject him, ink crawling off the page, because the names are already loose. Enraged, the room tries to take the whole school. Yara enters it deliberately, carrying the final name — her sister's — and offers herself as resident in exchange for release. Beat: sacrifice at the hinge.

chapters.title: Ida's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ida Voss's POV, inside the room. The children refuse the trade: they've waited fifty years to be returned, not swapped. Ida takes Yara's hand and walks her to the door, saying the room only ever held them because no one came back for them. Someone did. Beat: grace undoing the bargain.

chapters.title: Collapse
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The room folds inward as the last name is spoken; Aldridge, freed by the refusal of her signature's terms, chooses to stay behind and hold the door shut from the other side. The east wing's mirrors shatter outward, one second early this time. Beat: catharsis with a wound in it.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Documented
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Police find thirty sets of remains and a paper trail implicating four generations of administrators; Halloway is arrested. The town remembers, unwillingly, in newsprint and funerals. Yara's notebooks are intact except for every mention of her sister, now blank pages. Beat: victory audited against loss.

chapters.title: The Blank Page
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Grieving the erasure of her own memory, Yara visits her sister's grave and finds fresh flowers — left by whom? A new notebook entry appears in handwriting almost like hers: thank you. She understands some returns aren't losses. Beat: sorrow softened into mystery.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Epilogue, mixed POV. Blackfen reopens the east wing as a memorial archive; Yara becomes its archivist, cataloguing the recovered lives. On the last page of the ledger, beneath thirty names, a thirty-first line waits, unsigned — and Yara leaves it blank on purpose. Beat: vigilance as ongoing devotion.
